summary: Intro demo showing hosted chat/text generation basics with emphasis on latency vs throughput tradeoffs, streaming behavior, retry/backoff patterns, and an overview of the Redwood Console Optimize recommendations. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a clinical triage assistant; main concerns are sub-300ms tail latency for short responses, per-token cost, and SOC2/KMS for PHI.
topics: console cost/latency dashboards and Optimize suggestions
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick audio check?
[00:05] Alex (CTO): Audio good here.
[00:07] Jordan: Awesome. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood Inference, joined by Priya our sales engineer and Omar on solutions. today we'll run through a hosted API walkthrough focusing on latency vs throughput patterns and how the console helps you pick parameters and retries.
[00:25] Sam (Lead Eng): Great. high level we want a clinical triage assistant, short responses, sub 300ms p95 ideally for the 30-60 token responses. also cost targets.
[00:35] Priya (SE): Got it. sounds like we should cover streaming behavior (how tokens arrive), param tuning for short outputs, concurrency controls, and retry/backoff to handle transient errors. we'll demo console suggestions from Optimize as well.
[00:46] Jordan: Quick agenda: 1) quick API demo, 2) console tour — per-route latency/cost, 3) how retries and backoffs work, 4) Q&A and next steps.
[00:56] Maya (ML Eng): Also can you show how KV caching/prefix caching works? our prompts reuse a lot of boilerplate medical context.
[01:04] Priya: Absolutely, we'll cover prefix caching and how it reduces per-token work and latency.

[01:20] -- API live demo start --
[01:22] Priya: I'll paste a simple chat generation request. note we use streaming by default for lower tail latency; tokens come as a delta stream so clients can render early. here's a sample with max_tokens: 60, temperature: 0.2, top_p: 0.9.
[01:40] [Priya pastes curl sample into shared doc link: https://redwood.example/sandbox/rl-demo]
[01:45] Priya: When streaming, the SDK opens a chunked response so you typically see the first token in ~50-120ms depending on model + network. the bulk of our tuning is around model choice, batch windowing, and whether you accept partial results.
[02:02] Alex: ok so streaming helps tail but what about concurrency — if we have 100 parallel users, will streaming still keep p95 low?
[02:10] Omar: good question. streaming helps individual request latency; throughput is influenced by batching on the server. Redwood will automatically batch compatible requests within tight time windows to amortize GPU cost. if you need strict latency SLO you can set a small batch window or pin to dedicated capacity to avoid noisy neighbors.
[02:29] Sam: small batch window — does that increase token cost?
[02:32] Priya: It can. smaller batch windows reduce batching efficiency which increases GPU ops per token and thus cost. Optimize suggests batch/window settings based on your qps distribution.

[02:50] [00:03:12] Priya: demoing the Console: here is per-route token cost, p50/p95 latencies, and a heatmap of sequence lengths. you can click "Optimize" and get suggestions: quantize model to int8 for throughput, enable prefix cache for static context, and set recommended batch window.
[03:12] Maya: when you say prefix cache, is that server side? does it store user data?
[03:17] Priya: it's server-side ephemeral caching of KV pairs for a pinned prefix. it's not persisted to long-term storage unless you turn on session caching. and data plane encryption uses customer KMS if configured.
[03:28] Janelle (Security): for PHI we need SOC 2, key management, audit logs and the ability to run in our VPC. do you provide those?
[03:35] Jordan: Yes — Hosted API can integrate with customer-managed KMS and we have Clear SOC2 reports and audit logs. for full VPC/private deployment we also have Dedicated and Private options if you want an on-prem or VPC control plane.

[03:52] Sam: demo question — retries. our current stack treats any 5xx as a hard fail. how does Redwood recommend handling retries for streaming endpoints?
[03:59] Priya: For streaming, we recommend: 1) client-side incremental checkpoints (render partial tokens), 2) on connection failures attempt a reconnect with exponential backoff and resume from last stable token when possible, 3) for generation aborts return an error and consider fallback to a cheaper model or cached answer. our SDK supports resumable streams for many models; on the server side we also support idempotency keys to avoid double-charging.
[04:21] Alex: resume from last stable token — how reliable is that?
[04:24] Priya: it depends on model state. we keep an internal KV cache of attended tokens, and with idempotency + the same temperature/top_p you can often get a compatible continuation, but it's not guaranteed word-for-word. for strict determinism you'd use deterministic sampling settings (temperature 0, top_p 1) or use a rerank/fallback.

[04:44] [00:05:00] Jordan: quick whiteboard — latency contributors: network + model first-token time + decoding time + batching delay. main levers: choose a smaller model or quantized variant for lower per-token latency, reduce batch window, enable streaming, and use prefix KV to avoid re-encoding context.
[05:05] Sam: Any examples of numbers? like what does p95 look like for a 50-token response on medium model vs quantized small model?
[05:10] Priya: Rough ballpark from our benchmarks: non-quantized medium model p95 for short responses ~500-700ms on shared hosted; quantized small ~200-350ms; dedicated pinned capacity gets you lower variance and better tail behavior. we'll include our benchmark sheet.

[05:30] Maya: For our clinical content we need to ensure no cold-start spikes. how does autoscaling behave?
[05:35] Omar: autoscaling is governed by target throughput and a warm pool — you can configure reserved instances (Dedicated) or lean on hosted with pre-warmed workers. autoscaler uses predictive heuristics based on historical qps and can maintain a minimum warm pool to reduce cold starts.

[05:52] [00:06:25] Alex: cost question — do you charge on tokens or compute? we need to map to our cost model.
[05:58] Jordan: Hosted is per-token + model surcharge. Dedicated is a reserved capacity fee plus per-inference unit for excess. we provide a cost estimator in the console so you can run your workload through it. for short responses cost is dominated by per-request overhead unless you batch many small requests.

[06:15] Sam: what about rate limiting? we have bursty traffic from webhooks and mobile.
[06:20] Priya: Redwood supports per-key rate limits and leaky-bucket style throttles. you can set per-route quotas and graceful 429 handlers. we also support preflight quotas for canary traffic.

[06:35] [00:07:10] Jordan: quick demo — I'm toggling "Optimize" for a route with sample logs. it surfaces three suggestions: reduce batch window from 20ms->8ms for latency SLO, enable prefix cache, and try the int8 quantized variant for this model. clicking "apply" opens a rollout canary.
[07:00] Maya: can we A/B test different model variants?
[07:03] Priya: Yes — rollouts let you percent-split traffic across model variants and we show per-variant latency/cost. that can help pick the minimal model that meets quality.

[07:20] [00:07:50] Sam: on errors, if we fallback to a cheaper model does Redwood automatically re-score responses or do we do post-processing?
[07:27] Omar: you can configure automatic fallback policies — when primary model errors or latency spikes, traffic routes to fallback variant. for quality gating you can run a quick reranker on the fallback result or flag for human review.

[07:40] Janelle: security again — where are audit logs stored and how long retained?
[07:44] Jordan: Audit logs are available in the Console and via exports; retention is configurable. default hosted retention is 90 days; we can extend for enterprise. full audit trails include request metadata but not raw prompt content unless you enable logs for debugging. logs can be routed to your S3/GCS and encrypted with your KMS.

[08:05] [00:08:30] Alex: Do you have any notes on deterministic outputs? we need repeatability for some flows.
[08:10] Priya: Determinism: set temperature 0 and top_p 1, and keep sampling deterministic. also pin model version and seed where possible. note that quantized kernels and some optimizations may change tiny tokenization/decoding differences; for exact bit-for-bit repeatability you'd run the same model binary in a pinned environment.

[08:33] Maya: about the client SDK — does it handle streaming reconnects/backoff?
[08:37] Priya: Yes, SDKs include convenience helpers for reconnect, resume, and exponential backoff policies. they also emit metrics you can forward to your observability stack.

[08:50] [00:09:10] Jordan: let's run a quick synthetic: 60 token prompt at 30 qps. (Priya kicks off a sandbox job; shared link in chat).
[09:01] Priya: Running now... baseline results: p50 120ms, p95 420ms on hosted medium; enabling prefix cache drops p95 to 280ms; quantized variant p95 210ms but quality check needed.
[09:18] Sam: are those numbers from single AZ?
[09:20] Priya: yes single region; cross-region adds network latency.

[09:28] Alex: how does billing work for retries/reconnections? will we be double-billed if we reconnect?
[09:33] Jordan: we bill per generated token; for reconnects if the service replays tokens we use idempotency keys to avoid double-charging where possible. if the client resends requests you may see duplicates; idempotency and resumable streams are the recommended pattern.

[09:48] [00:10:05] Janelle: can you share SOC2 and encryption whitepapers and the network diagram?
[09:54] Jordan: Yes, I'll send SOC2, KMS integration notes and a network topology. Priya will include the benchmark sheet and a suggested config for your workload.

[10:05] Maya: one last question — if we start hosted and later move to Dedicated, how smooth is the migration?
[10:10] Omar: it's designed to be low-friction. you keep same API surface; model catalog and pins carry over. Dedicated gives you reserved GPUs and lower tail variance. the Console and rollouts work across modes.

[10:24] [00:11:03] Alex: ok good recap please.
[10:28] Jordan: Recap: We showed streaming behavior, param knobs for short responses, retry/resume recommendations, console Optimize suggestions (batch window, prefix cache, quantize), security checklist coverage, and next steps: we'll send pricing and a benchmark template, Priya to spin up 24h sandbox and run baseline, customer to share sample prompts.
[10:45] Sam: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[10:48] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up with the doc links and calendar invite for POC kickoff.

[10:55] -- meeting ends --

Note: transcript contains occasional ASR mis-hearings (e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache, "OtherCloud A I" for OtherCloudAI) and some speaker labels auto-attributed.
